In Postgres Enterprise Manager (PEM), several SECURITY DEFINER functions in the pem schema of the PEM backend database are owned by a superuser but do not set a safe search_path. Any PEM user who can connect to the PEM backend database can create objects that these functions use in place of the intended ones, and so run arbitrary SQL with superuser privileges. Temporary objects can be used for this on every supported PostgreSQL version, and objects in the public schema on PostgreSQL 14 backends and backends upgraded from PostgreSQL 14.
From PEM 10.6.1, these functions run with a fixed search_path.

From PEM 10.6.1, the SQL Profiler only reads and writes files inside the user's storage directory.

In Postgres Enterprise Manager (PEM), webhook URLs are not validated, and the PEM agent does not restrict the URL schemes it uses to deliver webhooks. A user with the alert configuration role (pem_config_alert) can set up a webhook with a file:// URL. When the webhook is sent, the agent on the PEM server, which runs as root by default, reads the local file and stores its contents in the webhook error record in the PEM database, where any PEM user can read it.
From PEM 10.6.1, PEM accepts and sends only http and https webhook URLs.

In Postgres Enterprise Manager (PEM), any PEM user can run the pem.send_webhook() function, which runs with elevated privileges and queues a payload for any configured webhook. From PEM 10.6.1, no PEM login role can call this function directly. PEM still sends webhook notifications through its own internal paths.

Validating an untrusted ISO 8601 duration string into a timedelta field with Pydantic V1 takes quadratic time: an input of a few dozen kilobytes takes seconds to validate.

The iso8601_duration_re regular expression used to parse ISO 8601 durations (in pydantic/datetime_parse.py) contains an unescaped ".", which also matches digits. On a string of digits, the repeated groups overlap and the regex engine backtracks in quadratic time.

The issue was fixed in commit 62791e66a9f8f118e465ed760c9e2ede9ae3055e. Users relying on the pydantic.v1 namespace in Pydantic V2 should upgrade to 2.14.2 or later.

Impact: denial of service through validation of untrusted input. Affected are applications validating untrusted strings into timedelta fields.

Validating an untrusted list into a field constrained with unique_items=True with Pydantic V1 takes quadratic time: an input of a few hundred kilobytes takes seconds to validate.

The ConstrainedList.unique_items_validator validator (in pydantic/types.py) checks each item against all the following ones. For a list with no duplicates (the common, valid case), this results in a quadratic number of comparisons.

The issue was fixed in commit 6ec75e57f277a820ec583e601167f25fe8dc7c87. Users relying on the pydantic.v1 namespace in Pydantic V2 should upgrade to 2.14.2 or later.

Impact: denial of service through validation of untrusted input. Affected are applications validating untrusted lists into fields constrained with unique_items=True (using conlist() or Field()).

The fix only applies to lists of builtin scalar types (int, float, str, bytes, bool and None), for which duplicates can be detected in linear time. Lists of other types (e.g. models or dictionaries) are still checked in quadratic time, as their items aren't guaranteed to be hashable: bound their size using the max_items constraint.

Pydantic V2 models are not affected.

When extra data is allowed, providing both the alias and the name of an aliased TypedDict or dataclass field makes the unvalidated value (provided under the name) overwrite the validated one (provided under the alias), resulting in validated data not matching the declared type.

Extra items are stored in the same dictionary as the fields (the returned dictionary for TypedDict, the instance __dict__ for dataclasses). As only the alias is marked as used, the field name is treated as an extra item, and its unvalidated value overrides the validated one. The TypedDict validator (pydantic-core/src/validators/typed_dict.rs) and the dataclass validator (pydantic-core/src/validators/dataclass.rs) share this logic.

The issue was fixed in commit 34491f5328f168f14e3769cd5f0f83c0af0f4778.

Impact: validation bypass, as data returned by validation doesn't match the declared type. Affected are applications validating untrusted data into TypedDict or dataclass types with aliased fields and extra data allowed (with extra='allow', or with the extra_items argument for TypedDict), using Pydantic V2 (up to and including 2.14.1).

Pydantic models (BaseModel) are not affected, as extra data is stored separately from fields.

Validating an untrusted string in exponent notation into a Fraction field computes the full power of ten without any bound: an input of a few bytes takes seconds to validate.

String inputs are passed to the Fraction constructor. For strings in exponent notation (e.g. '1e8000000'), CPython computes the corresponding power of ten as an integer (in Lib/fractions.py).

The issue was fixed in commit 69ed168e9ad465eef4c8d81efb152a93b604daf5. For strings in exponent notation, the exponent is now parsed before calling the Fraction constructor, and exponents larger than 4300 (in absolute value) are rejected.

Impact: denial of service through validation of untrusted input. Affected are applications validating untrusted strings into Fraction fields (in both JSON and Python mode, including in strict mode), using Pydantic from 2.10.0 up to (but excluding) 2.14.0.

From 2.14.0, exponents larger than 4300 (in absolute value) are rejected, matching the maximum number of digits accepted for integers.

Validating an untrusted URL with a long scheme and many hosts into a multi-host URL field (e.g. PostgresDsn) takes quadratic time and memory: an input of about a hundred kilobytes takes around a gigabyte of memory to validate.

The parse_multihost_url() function (in pydantic-core/src/validators/url.rs) parses each host separately, prepending the whole URL prefix (including the scheme) to every one of them. As the scheme can be arbitrarily long, and is parsed and stored once per host, both time and memory grow quadratically with the input size. Allowed schemes (e.g. postgres for PostgresDsn) are only checked after parsing, so they don't prevent the issue.

The issue was fixed in commit b4028f9d87e34750e53be0ba011d70f3c0fcc94e.

Impact: denial of service through validation of untrusted input. Affected are applications validating untrusted strings into multi-host URL fields (PostgresDsn, MongoDsn, NatsDsn, or custom types built on MultiHostUrl).

When validating JSON data into a model allowing extra data, the keys of extra data aren't validated against the key type annotated on __pydantic_extra__, resulting in extra data not matching the declared type. This is the case if you define __pydantic_extra__ as e.g. dict[Annotated[str, Field(pattern=r'^x_')], int].

The validate_json_by_iteration() method (in pydantic-core/src/validators/model_fields.rs), used to validate JSON data into models, only validates the values of extra data, and stores the keys as is.

The issue was fixed in commit 4c65dbda9970a488e2ff21c8693fc6f6d70a3358.

Impact: validation bypass, as extra data returned by validation doesn't match the declared type. Affected are applications validating untrusted JSON data into models allowing extra data (with extra='allow'), with a key type annotated on __pydantic_extra__ (e.g. dict[Annotated[str, Field(pattern=...)], int]), using Pydantic from 2.13.0 up to (but excluding) 2.14.2.

Python mode validation isn't affected.

previous.context: A flaw was found in Keycloak. This vulnerability allows an authenticated remote attacker to cause a denial of service by terminating active sessions of arbitrary users. When processing Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) documents that lack a root signature, Keycloak accepts the request as long as any assertion within the document is signed, without verifying its context or placement. An attacker holding a validly signed assertion can embed it into an unsigned logout request for another user, causing Keycloak to accept the forged request and terminate the victim's session.

This issue can expose restricted authentication endpoints intended only for internal access, though Keycloak's internal authentication mechanisms remain intact.

previous.context: In Dolibarr before 24.0.3, dolForgeSQLCriteriaCallback() in htdocs/core/lib/functions.lib.php allows account takeover because it strips only a single table-name prefix from a Universal Search Filter (sqlfilters) operand before checking it against the forbidden-field denylist (pass, pass_crypted, api_key). MariaDB and MySQL accept a two-level qualification such as schema.alias.column, so an operand of the form dolibarr.u.pass_crypted survives the check and is emitted into the WHERE clause. A remote authenticated user holding only the holiday read and readall permissions, which confer no user-management or administrative access, can use the resulting boolean oracle at GET /api/index.php/holidays to recover any user's bcrypt password hash and api_key one character at a time, including an administrator's. Because api_key is accepted directly by the REST API as a bearer credential, this yields full administrative control of the application. This bypasses the fix for CVE-2026-89012, which added only a strtolower() call and did not address prefix depth. The same denylist also omits pass_temp, which stores a password in cleartext, as well as national_registration_number, salary, birth, address, personal_mobile and note_private.

previous.context: When message history is serialized and loaded again, a tool result that contains a JSON object in the serialized shape of one of Pydantic AI's file types is rebuilt as that file. A third party who controls data a tool returns, such as a record that an MCP server or a function tool returns from an external system, can use this to make the application download a URL on its local network, or make the model provider read an s3:// object or uploaded file with the application's credentials. Applications are affected when tool results can contain third-party data, message history containing those results is serialized and loaded again (stored history, history a UI adapter holds on the server, or Temporal, DBOS or Prefect durable execution), and the model is one Pydantic AI downloads files for, one that honors force_download, or one whose provider resolves non-HTTP file URLs or uploaded files. History that a client submits through the Vercel AI or AG-UI adapter in the default mode is not affected. The issue is fixed in pydantic-ai and pydantic-ai-slim 1.107.10 and 2.66.0.

previous.context: A flaw was found in the Kuadrant WebAssembly (WASM) shim shipped in Red Hat Connectivity Link 1.5. previous.context: vulnerability-lookup prior to version 7.1.0 contains two security issues in its web interface. First, the /user/toggle_2fa endpoint accepted HTTP GET requests and disabled the authenticated user's two-factor authentication without requiring password confirmation. Because the state-changing operation was reachable via GET, an attacker with a basic account could embed an image element (or any other GET-triggering markup) in a comment pointing to that endpoint. When a victim with 2FA enabled viewed the comment, their browser silently issued the GET request, disabling the victim's second factor of authentication. No CSRF token was enforced on the GET path, and no password was required to confirm the action. Second, the comment detail page (/comment/<uuid>) rendered unpublished comments to any visitor who possessed the URL, bypassing the moderation workflow that was intended to keep such content hidden until approved. The API correctly restricted access, but the web view did not enforce the same authorization check. The combined effect allows an attacker to degrade a victim's account security (removal of 2FA) through a single page view and to read content that was not yet approved for public release.

previous.context:
Flowintel's community data launcher script passes the admin API key as a command-line argument to a child Python helper process. On Unix-like systems, process arguments are readable by all local users via standard tools such as ps or by reading /proc/<pid>/cmdline, allowing any local user to observe the key while the helper process is running.

An attacker with local access to the host can capture the admin API key during the brief window in which the helper process is active. Possession of the key grants full administrative access to the Flowintel REST API, enabling unauthorized creation, modification, or deletion of threat intelligence data, users, roles, and organisations.

Preconditions:
- The victim must invoke the community data import or deletion command (launch.sh -tdc or -dtdc) with the API key supplied as a positional argument.
- The attacker must have a local user account on the same host and be able to observe process listings during the helper execution window.

Impact:
- Disclosure of the Flowintel admin API key to any local user.
- Subsequent full administrative control over the Flowintel instance via its REST API.

Affected: <4.1.0

Flowintel's template repository subsystem did not adequately constrain file access to the configured repository base directory. Two related weaknesses existed:

- Repository registration and editing accepted arbitrary local paths without verifying they resolved inside the configured REPOSITORY_BASE_PATH, allowing an authenticated user to point a repository at any readable directory on the host.
- Manifest and template file lookups used normalized (non-canonical) path joins and a startswith-based guard that could be bypassed by symbolic links, permitting reads of files outside the intended repository.

An authenticated user with the ability to add or edit a template repository could therefore cause the application to read and return the contents of arbitrary files readable by the service account, including configuration files, credentials, or other sensitive data.

Affected: Flowintel versions prior to 4.1.0.

FlowIntel contains a resource exhaustion vulnerability in its file-to-note conversion feature. When a user converts an attached CSV or JSON file into a case note, the application renders the data as a Markdown table by padding every row to the maximum column count. A crafted file with a small number of filled cells but a very large number of columns (or keys) causes the application to allocate a quadratic number of padded table cells, potentially exhausting a worker process in memory or CPU.

The same issue affects nested JSON values rendered inside table cells, where pretty-printed indentation further inflates the output size.

Preconditions:
- An authenticated user with access to a case in FlowIntel
- Ability to attach and convert a CSV or JSON file to a note

Impact:
- Denial of service: exhaustion of a worker process, potentially disrupting service for other users
- No confidentiality or integrity impact

Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0

previous.context:
flowintel contains a log injection vulnerability in its case history (audit log) subsystem. The case history is stored as a line-delimited file where each line represents a single event attributed to a specific user. User-controlled fields, including user names, event messages, and case titles used during case merging, were written to the history file without sanitizing embedded line separator characters (such as carriage return, line feed, vertical tab, form feed, and Unicode line/paragraph separators).

An authenticated user with the ability to create or modify case history entries could embed line separators in these fields. Upon writing, the injected separators would split a single intended entry into multiple lines, each of which the history format interprets as a distinct event. This allows an attacker to forge additional history entries attributed to arbitrary users, corrupting the audit trail and undermining the integrity of case records.

The vulnerability affects the case history append and merge operations. No authentication bypass or privilege escalation is required beyond normal case-management access.

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0.

- Potential unauthorized read access to source code and repository metadata

FlowIntel contains multiple security flaws in its note variable resolution, chatbot API tooling, and AI report generation.

- Note variable references (e.g. cross-case or cross-task lookups) were resolved using the viewing user's privileges rather than the destination case's audience. An authenticated user with access to a shared or imported note could embed references to private cases, causing sensitive case data to be pulled into AI report requests, exports, and MISP sends without the referenced case's audience having granted read access.

- The chatbot API tool permitted the language model to invoke any FlowIntel API endpoint, including administrative routes and state-changing GET operations, without an allow-list or path validation. An attacker who can influence the model's instructions (e.g. via untrusted case content) could induce data modification or access restricted endpoints.

- AI report generation passed the Ollama bearer token and full case content as command-line arguments to a child process, exposing them in the system process table to any local user.

Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0.

previous.context:
Flowintel disabled TLS certificate verification for all MISP API connections and used unverified SSL contexts for IMAP and SMTP STARTTLS mail connections. This allowed an on-path (man-in-the-middle) attacker positioned between Flowintel and its MISP or mail servers to impersonate the remote server and intercept sensitive data.

Affected connections include:
- All MISP HTTPS API calls (event retrieval, attribute search, event creation, connectivity checks, and API validation)
- SMTP STARTTLS connections used for sending email notifications
- IMAP TLS connections used for fetching mail archives and testing connectivity

An attacker who can observe or intercept network traffic between Flowintel and the MISP or mail server could:
- Capture MISP API keys and mail credentials (SMTP/IMAP passwords)
- Read all threat intelligence data exchanged (events, attributes, objects, reports)
- Inject or modify threat intelligence data returned to Flowintel

The vulnerability required no authentication on the part of the attacker and no user interaction; it was exploitable by any party with a network position between Flowintel and its configured MISP or mail endpoints.

Affected versions: Flowintel prior to 4.1.0.

previous.context:
FlowIntel contained a Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) vulnerability affecting fourteen web routes that performed destructive or state-changing operations. The affected routes accepted HTTP GET requests in addition to (or instead of) POST, which bypassed the Flask-WTF CSRF token validation that is only enforced on non-GET requests.

The vulnerable operations included:
- Case deletion and case merging
- Organisation removal from a case
- Task deletion (case and template)
- Case template and note template deletion
- Connector, connector instance, and icon deletion
- Custom tag deletion and status change
- Taxonomy and galaxy status changes

An attacker who could induce an authenticated user to follow a crafted link or load a page containing a cross-site navigation (e.g., an image tag or redirect) could trigger any of these destructive actions using the victim's session cookie, without the victim's explicit consent or awareness. No special privileges beyond a valid authenticated session with the appropriate role (editor or admin) were required on the victim's account.

Security impact: unauthorized deletion or modification of cases, tasks, templates, connectors, icons, custom tags, taxonomies, and galaxies belonging to the victim or the organisation, resulting in loss of data integrity.

Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0

previous.context:
Flowintel , contained a session management vulnerability in its browser authentication mechanism. The session identifier used a bare numeric user ID rather than a credential-bound token, resulting in several related weaknesses:

- Remembered logins (remember-me cookies) remained valid after a user changed their password, allowing an attacker holding a previously issued cookie to retain access indefinitely.
- Server-side session identifiers were not rotated upon login (local, SSO, or remembered), enabling session fixation.
- Self-service email and password changes did not require verification of the current password, permitting an attacker with an active session to modify account credentials without knowledge of the existing password.
- Administrator-initiated password resets did not revoke other browser sessions, invalidate remembered logins, or rotate the affected user's API key.

An attacker who obtained a valid session or remember-me cookie (e.g., through XSS, network interception, or cookie theft) could maintain unauthorized access even after the legitimate user changed their password. Additionally, an attacker with any valid session could change the account's email address or password without knowing the current credentials, effectively taking over the account.

Affected versions: Flowintel prior to 4.1.0.

previous.context:
Flowintel contains a privilege escalation vulnerability in its Matrix relay (bot) integration. When the relay forwarded API requests on behalf of a represented user, the authorization and permission checks evaluated the relay bot's elevated role while the request handlers acted as the lower-privileged represented user. This mismatch allowed users with restricted roles (e.g., Read Only) to perform write operations, directory lookups, calendar modifications, assignment changes, template creation, and import actions they were not authorized to perform.

Additionally, relay authority was determined by matching editable user profile fields (name and email) rather than a protected, non-spoofable identifier. An ordinary user who modified their profile to match the expected bot name could be recognized as the trusted relay, enabling impersonation of the bot and potential access to its elevated privileges.

Preconditions:
- A valid Flowintel user account with a restricted role (e.g., Read Only)
- Access to the Matrix relay integration or the ability to send API requests with the relay's API key and a MATRIX-ID header
- For the impersonation vector: ability to edit one's own profile name fields

Security impact:
- Unauthorized write operations by users with read-only or otherwise restricted permissions
- Potential impersonation of the trusted relay bot by ordinary users
- Bypass of organization-level access controls and role-based restrictions
- Unauthorized modification of cases, tasks, calendar events, templates, and user directory entries

Affected versions: Flowintel prior to 4.1.0

Flowintel contains multiple SSO identity and organisation trust boundary violations that collectively allow account takeover, privilege escalation, and unauthorized access to private case data.

- Keycloak SSO accepted unverified email claims, and all SSO providers (Keycloak, Entra ID, SimpleSAML) could resolve a claimed email address to an existing account that was created via a different sign-in method, enabling cross-provider account collision and unauthorized access to another user's account and data.

- Entra ID role mapping relied on group display names, which tenant members could duplicate by creating a group with the same name as a privileged group (e.g. FlowintelAdmin), resulting in unauthorized role escalation.

- SSO provisioning reused organisations whose display names matched user-controlled profile names, granting the new SSO user access to that organisation's private cases without explicit administrator assignment.

- Case sharing via the API resolved organisations by name using a first-match query, so ambiguous names could silently resolve to the wrong organisation.

Preconditions: an attacker must have a valid SSO identity (Keycloak, Entra ID, or SimpleSAML) or be a member of the relevant Entra tenant. No local administrator access is required.

Security impact: unauthorized access to private case data, privilege escalation to Editor or higher roles, and account takeover across authentication providers.

Affected versions: Flowintel prior to 4.1.0.

FlowIntel contains an authorization bypass in its user directory and assignment endpoints that allows authenticated users to access data belonging to other organisations.

When the LIMIT_USER_VIEW_TO_ORG setting is enabled to restrict directory visibility to the caller's organisation, several API endpoints (user lookup by ID, last name, Matrix ID, and role-based listings) did not consistently enforce the organisation boundary. An authenticated non-admin user could retrieve profiles of users in other organisations by supplying their identifiers.

Additionally, OrgAdmin users could retrieve the task assignments of any user in the system, including tasks and case titles from private cases to which they had no access. The assignment endpoints did not verify that the requested user belonged to the caller's organisation or that the underlying cases were visible to the caller.

Security impact:
- Exposure of user identities (names, Matrix IDs, roles) across organisation boundaries
- Disclosure of task assignments, case titles, and workflow details from private cases
- Potential enumeration of other organisations' membership and case activity

FlowIntel contains multiple authorization and credential management vulnerabilities affecting connector instances, MISP helper tools, and case templates.

- Connector instance metadata, connectivity checks, and case listings accepted instance IDs without verifying if the acting user had visibility or ownership rights, allowing unauthorized access to sensitive configuration and data.
- Case template serialization and creation processes exposed connector instances attached to templates regardless of the user's permissions, potentially leaking credentials or instance details to users who should not have access.
- Editing connector instances allowed changes to URLs or sharing scopes without requiring re-authentication of API keys, enabling the reuse of another user's credentials in a new context or the leakage of shared keys to unauthorized endpoints.

previous.context:
flowintel contains an Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) vulnerability affecting multiple endpoints that manage child records of cases and tasks. An authenticated user with access to one case or task could read or modify records belonging to other cases by supplying identifiers of those records directly in the request.

Affected operations include:
- Reading task notes, subtasks, and URL tools by referencing their IDs without verifying they belong to the authorized task
- Retrieving task assignees for a task belonging to a different case
- Editing or deleting timeline events and timeline event links belonging to another case
- Editing or removing case connectors belonging to another case
- Invoking connector module operations (MISP, generic connectors, worker calls) by combining an authorized case with a connector link from a different case

The root cause is that the application authorized the parent resource (case or task) in the URL but then fetched or operated on the child record independently without verifying the child's ownership relationship to the authorized parent.

Security impact: an authenticated user can exfiltrate sensitive threat intelligence data from cases they do not have access to, and can modify or delete timeline entries, connector configurations, and other records in unauthorized cases, leading to data integrity loss and potential disruption of incident response workflows.

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0

previous.context:
flowintel contains multiple related flaws that allow an authenticated attacker to inject arbitrary HTML or script into pages viewed by other users.

- Timeline rendering: the timeline library's autolinking feature rewrote already-sanitised case notes and imported MISP attribute values into generated HTML link elements. Crafted text containing quote characters could break out of the generated attribute context, altering the surrounding markup and enabling script execution in the victim's browser.

- Search highlighting: the highlight injection logic used a regular expression to locate text between angle brackets and spliced <mark> elements into the resulting string. Because the pattern could match inside HTML attribute values, the rewrite could corrupt or inject content into attributes of already-sanitised markup, again leading to DOM-based cross-site scripting.

- Content-Type confusion: three analyser selection endpoints returned session-stored JSON strings with a text/html content type. A browser receiving such a response will parse and render the body as HTML, so any HTML or script embedded in the stored value is executed in the victim's context.

Preconditions: the attacker must be an authenticated user with the ability to create or import case content (notes, MISP attributes) containing specially crafted quote or angle-bracket sequences. The victim must subsequently open the affected case timeline, run a search, or request one of the selection endpoints.

Impact: successful exploitation yields DOM-based cross-site scripting in the victim's browser session, potentially allowing disclosure of case data, session manipulation, or execution of arbitrary actions under the victim's identity.

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0.

The system failed to enforce the required Admin or Case Admin privilege check before performing this case revival side effect.

A user with basic task-level permissions (e.g., editor, queuer, or queue admin) could trigger the revival of a completed privileged case through the browser interface or the REST API, without holding the elevated role required for case-level operations. This could disrupt case lifecycle management, clear completion metadata, and potentially expose the case to further unauthorized modifications.

The vulnerability affects both the browser-based task completion/status-change endpoints and the corresponding API endpoints, as well as the task creation flow.

Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0.

previous.context:
flowintel contains an authorization bypass in the browser-based admin user editing interface. The edit_user view in the admin panel verified that a non-platform-admin user could only edit accounts belonging to their own organization, but it did not verify that the target account was not a platform-admin account. As a result, an authenticated user holding an organization-admin role could open the edit form for any platform-admin account and submit modifications, including changes to credentials, roles, or other account attributes.

The API layer already enforced a restriction preventing non-admin users from targeting admin accounts, but the browser-based admin view lacked the equivalent check, creating an inconsistent authorization boundary.

Impact:
- Unauthorized modification of platform-admin account data (integrity)
- Potential lockout or privilege manipulation of platform administrators (availability)
- Escalation of an organization-admin role to effectively control platform-level administration

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0.

previous.context:
flowintel contains an authorization flaw in its user deletion functionality. Organization-scoped administrators (org admins) are able to delete platform-level administrator accounts through both the browser-based admin interface and the REST API.

The existing authorization logic verified that an org admin could only target users within their own organization, but it did not enforce the privilege hierarchy between organization admins and platform admins. As a result, an authenticated org admin could issue a deletion request against any platform-admin account belonging to the same organization, causing the target account, its sessions, and related records to be permanently removed.

Impact:
- Loss of platform-level administrative oversight
- Potential disruption of platform-wide management functions
- Removal of higher-privilege accounts that should be protected from lower-privilege roles

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0

previous.context:
A vulnerability exists in the flowintel application's calendar functionality that allows unauthorized access to private case data. The task calendar queries failed to enforce visibility checks on the parent case associated with tasks. Specifically, tasks assigned to a user or belonging to the user's organization were returned in calendar views (including browser and API ICS feeds) without verifying whether the user had permission to view the parent case. This allowed users to potentially discover and access details of private cases they were not authorized to view, leading to information disclosure.

The issue affected the default task visibility logic and the assigned-only task queries. The fix ensures that case visibility is rechecked in addition to task assignment or organization membership, preventing the exposure of private case data in calendar outputs.

Affected versions: flowintel < 4.1.0

previous.context:
flowintel contains an authorization flaw in its recurring reminder notification subsystem. When a user is subscribed to recurring notifications for a case, the system does not re-verify the recipient's current access rights to that case before generating or displaying the notification.

As a result, a user who previously had access to a private case and later had that access revoked can still:
- Receive recurring reminder notifications containing case-related content.
- View stored reminder notifications in their notification list, including notification counts, even though they no longer have permission to view the underlying case.

The vulnerability affects both the notification creation path (recurring reminder generation) and the notification display path (listing and counting stored reminders). The issue arises because the authorization check performed at subscription time is not re-applied at delivery or retrieval time.

Security impact is limited to information disclosure: an unauthorized user may observe case titles, reminder messages, and associated metadata that they no longer have permission to access. No integrity or availability impact is indicated by the patch.

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0.

previous.context:
FlowIntel's alerting module contained an authorization bypass in the alert access control logic. When an alert was linked to a private case, the system relied solely on connector ownership (user or organization) to determine access, without verifying that the requesting user still held valid membership in the associated private case.

This meant that a user who was a connector owner of an alert could continue to read alert details, review history, raw payloads, and action comments, and could perform review-status updates or case-creation actions, even after their access to the linked private case had been revoked or they were never a member of that case.

Additionally, a time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) gap existed: after a review-status update or a competing case-creation claim was committed, the response could disclose private case identifiers or review history to a user whose access had been concurrently removed by another session linking the alert to a private case.

Impact:
- Unauthorized disclosure of private case data (review comments, raw payloads, action history) through alert endpoints.
- Unauthorized modification of alert review status and creation of cases from alerts the user should no longer access.
- Leakage of a competing case identifier to an unauthorized user during concurrent case-creation races.

Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0.

previous.context:
flowintel is a case management application that enforces an approval workflow for tasks in privileged cases. Tasks in such cases are required to start in a Requested status, meaning they must receive explicit approval before becoming active.

A logic flaw in the task-creation path allowed tasks to be initialized with a Created status (bypassing the approval step) in two scenarios:

- When a task was created from a template and no acting user was supplied, the privileged-case check was skipped entirely, leaving the task in Created status.
- When a case was created from a template, all copied tasks were unconditionally assigned the Created status regardless of the case's privileged designation.

An authenticated user with the ability to create tasks from templates or to instantiate cases from templates could therefore place tasks directly into an active state within privileged cases, circumventing the intended approval gate. This may expose restricted case content or permit actions that should require supervisory sign-off.

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0.

previous.context:
FlowIntel's chatbot component used a single shared MCP (Model Context Protocol) session and process-wide environment variable to pass per-user API credentials to a child process. Because the session and the ambient FLOWINTEL_API_KEY environment variable were shared across all concurrent requests, a user's authenticated identity could be applied to another user's tool invocation, or a stale/ambient credential could be inherited by a new request.

Preconditions:
- An authenticated user with access to the chatbot interface.
- Concurrent or overlapping chatbot tool invocations from different users, or a request made after another user's credentials were written to the process environment.

Impact:
- A lower-privilege user could read data belonging to a higher-privilege user (e.g., private investigation cases).
- A user whose session was invalidated (deleted, password changed, key revoked) could still operate under a previously cached ambient credential.
- The parent process environment was mutated with user-specific secrets, creating a persistent credential leak surface.

Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0.

previous.context:
flowintel contains a vulnerability in the case and task classification usage endpoints that allows authenticated users to view classification data associated with cases they do not have permission to access.

The affected endpoints, which provide lists of used taxonomies, tags, galaxies, clusters, and custom tags, did not properly enforce object-level access controls. While the endpoints required authentication, they failed to filter the returned data based on the requesting user's visibility permissions for the underlying cases. This allowed any authenticated user to enumerate classification usage across all cases, including private or restricted cases belonging to other organizations or users.

This issue could lead to the disclosure of sensitive information, such as the existence of specific cases, the types of threats or indicators associated with them, and the relationships between different classification elements, potentially aiding an attacker in reconnaissance or targeting.

Affected versions: < 4.1.0

previous.context:
flowintel contains an information disclosure vulnerability in its case history feature. When a user views the history of a case they are authorized to access, the history output includes references to other cases (linked, unlinked, or forked) without verifying whether the requesting user has permission to view those referenced cases. This exposes the identifiers and titles of cases that the user should not be able to discover.

The vulnerability affects multiple output paths:
- Browser-based case history view
- API history endpoint
- Plain-text history download
- Markdown history download
- Report timeline generation

An authenticated user with access to any single case can enumerate the existence and identifiers of other cases by reading the history of a case they can access. This bypasses the intended per-case access control model and may reveal the existence of sensitive investigations, their identifiers, and associated metadata to unauthorized users.

The raw audit storage is not modified; the issue is solely in the presentation layer failing to filter references to inaccessible cases before returning history data to the user.

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0.

previous.context: The WP Duplicate – WordPress Migration Plugin plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Remote Code Execution in all versions up to, and including, 1.1.11 via the save_single_batch_file function. This is due to a PHP type-juggling authentication bypass via loose != comparison with no is_string() guard, combined with unsanitized base64-decoded path construction in save_single_batch_file() lacking any directory traversal containment. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with custom-level access and above, to execute code on the server. Exploitation requires that the site owner has completed the plugin's initial setup so that the site_type and prod_key_random_id options are non-empty, though any non-empty secret value is bypassable via the type-juggling flaw.

This High severity Path Traversal (Arbitrary Read/Write) vulnerability known as CVE-2026-21592 was introduced in version 4.9.0.

This Path Traversal (Arbitrary Read/Write) vulnerability, with a CVSS Score of 7.7 and a CVSS Vector of CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:N/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N/E:P allows an unauthenticated attacker to disclose protected application configuration files, which has high impact to confidentiality, no impact to integrity, no impact to availability, and requires no user interaction.

Atlassian recommends that Crucible Server customers upgrade to the latest version. If you are unable to do so, upgrade your instance to the specified supported fixed version:
 Crucible Server 4.9: Upgrade to a release greater than or equal to 4.9.16

See the Crucible Server release notes ([https://confluence.atlassian.com/crucible/crucible-releases-298977378.html]). You can download the latest version of Crucible from the Crucible Download Archives ([https://www.atlassian.com/software/crucible/download-archives]).

The following description summarizes the vulnerability reported via our Penetration Testing program:

Crucible do not account for path parameters when validating protected paths requested through the static-resource route. A crafted path segment passes validation, after which Jetty removes the path parameter during dispatch and resolves the request to a protected resource. This can expose files under WEB-INF and permit direct invocation of admin-area JSPs outside the normal interceptor and administrative password checks. An ordinary authenticated user can exploit the issue, and unauthenticated exploitation is possible when anonymous access is enabled.

This Path Traversal (Arbitrary Read/Write) vulnerability, with a CVSS Score of 8.7 and a CVSS Vector of CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:N/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N allows an unauthenticated attacker to expose assets in your environment susceptible to exploitation, which has high impact to confidentiality, no impact to integrity, no impact to availability, and requires no user interaction.

Atlassian recommends that Confluence Data Center and Server customers upgrade to the latest version. If you are unable to do so, upgrade your instance to one of the specified supported fixed versions:
 Confluence Data Center 11.0: Upgrade to a release greater than or equal to 11.0.1
 Confluence Data Center 10.2: Upgrade to a release greater than or equal to 10.2.20
 Confluence Data Center 9.2: Upgrade to a release greater than or equal to 9.2.27

See the release notes ([https://confluence.atlassian.com/doc/confluence-release-notes-327.html]). You can download the
latest version of Confluence Data Center and Server from the download center
([https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence/download-archives]).

The following description summarizes the vulnerability reported internally:

Confluence CssServlet forwards a request-controlled path to ServletRequest.getRequestDispatcher. The dispatcher URL-decodes and normalizes the path, allowing an unauthenticated attacker to use an encoded traversal sequence to access protected web application resources such as /WEB-INF/web.xml. The demonstrated impact is disclosure of protected files that may contain configuration or secrets; no integrity or availability impact was demonstrated.

previous.context: Reposilite is lightweight and easy-to-use repository management software dedicated to Maven-based artifacts in the JVM ecosystem. From 3.5.16 until 3.6.0, as stated by the advisory, the Maven directory-index page interpolates the request URI without HTML escaping in its title, heading, base URL, and parent-directory link. The advisory says the content-embedded ctx.uri() is percent-encoded, preventing tag injection, but that a single quote passes through and breaks the quoted Parent-Directory link; it also says Location.of strips single quotes, so the reachability of the described quote-based trigger remains unresolved. The listing shares the Admin UI origin and does not set the sandbox Content-Security-Policy used for artifact and Javadoc responses, so the reported script execution could access a user's local-storage token. A manager token could enable full instance compromise. The advisory reports version 3.6.0 as fixed.

previous.context:
Missing Authorization vulnerability in the Apache Iggy server. The system snapshot command (GetSnapshot on the binary transports and POST /snapshot on HTTP) checked only that the caller was logged in, not the read_servers or manage_servers permission. Any authenticated user, including a user with no permissions, could download a diagnostic archive with the server log files, the host process list, a file system listing and the runtime server configuration. The runtime configuration contains the HTTP JWT signing secret and the message encryption key when they are set in the configuration. If HTTP is enabled, the user could use the signing secret to create tokens for any account, including root.

This issue affects Apache Iggy: before 0.9.0.

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 0.10.0, which fixes the issue.

previous.context: XWiki Platform is a generic wiki platform. From 4.3-milestone-1 until 16.10.18, 17.10.5, and 18.2.0, the /rest/wikis/{wikiName}/query REST endpoint permits HQL query construction that can combine blind conditions with FROM-clause injection to join BaseObject and StringProperty, bypassing the SELECT-column whitelist. An unauthenticated attacker can recover database values from inaccessible pages, including salted SHA1 password hashes and passwords stored in configuration properties. It should be assumed that, with more complex techniques, this can work even when the attacker cannot read any wiki page. A typical password hash may require roughly 800 requests, and expensive injected queries can also degrade availability. The issue is remediated by disabling HQL and XWQL REST queries by default. This issue is fixed in versions 16.10.18, 17.10.5, and 18.2.0.

previous.context: netty-incubator-codec-ohttp implements Oblivious HTTP (OHTTP) gateway and client functionality using Netty. Prior to 0.0.23.Final, BinaryHttpParser in codec-bhttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/bhttp/BinaryHttpParser.java accumulates attacker-controlled Binary HTTP variable-length integers into the int offset sumBytes. BinaryHttpParser.readRequestHead, BinaryHttpParser.readFieldLine, and BinaryHttpParser.getIndeterminateLength can narrow long lengths into that offset, causing integer wraparound before buffer indices are calculated. A remote peer that supplies a valid large encoded length to BinaryHttpParser or BinaryHttpDecoder can trigger an unchecked bounds exception from a small malformed message, fail or close the channel, and repeatedly cause denial of service. Java and Netty bounds checks prevent memory corruption, and no information disclosure was observed. This issue is fixed in version 0.0.23.Final.

From 0.0.20.Final until 0.0.27.Final, OHttpClientCodec in codec-ohttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/ohttp/OHttpClientCodec.java and OHttpServerCodec in codec-ohttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/ohttp/OHttpServerCodec.java retain the consumed outer cumulationBuffer after a valid OHTTP exchange completes, even though OHttpRequestResponseContext.destroy in codec-ohttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/ohttp/OHttpRequestResponseContext.java releases the inner Binary HTTP cumulation and the channel remains active. A peer can complete a large request or response and leave the keep-alive connection idle, causing the client and server handlers to retain the current high-water pooled or direct buffer capacity until later inbound content replaces it or the handler is removed. Many long-lived idle connections can pin substantial memory and create availability pressure. The issue does not cause unbounded growth for repeated exchanges on a single channel. This issue is fixed in version 0.0.27.Final.

previous.context:
Apache Shiro is vulnerable to session fixation when a user is authenticated via the "Remember me" functionality. In affected versions, when a subject is restored from a "Remember me" cookie, the existing session is not invalidated, nor is a new session created with a new ID.
Additionally, session IDs were accepted from the request URL even when session ID URL rewriting was disabled.
This issue affects all Apache Shiro versions through 3.0.0, only when RememberMe functionality is enabled.

Mitigation: Upgrade to version 3.0.1 or later, which fixes the issue by invalidating the existing session and creating a new session with a new ID when a subject is restored from a "Remember me" cookie, and by ignoring session IDs in the URL when URL rewriting is disabled.

previous.context:
Authorization annotations, such as @RequiresRoles and @RequiresPermissions, are not always enforced in some class or interface hierarchies.
Annotations declared on an interface were not enforced when using the shiro-guice, shiro-aspectj, shiro-cdi or shiro-jakarta-ee modules.
In addition, annotations declared on a class or a superclass were not always enforced when using shiro-guice or shiro-aspectj, allowing an unauthorized caller to invoke methods that should be protected.
This issue affects all Apache Shiro versions through 3.0.1, with impact depending on module and where annotations are declared.

Mitigation: Upgrade to version 3.0.2 or later, which fixes the issue. The annotation closest to the invoked method now takes precedence.
Alternatively, declare authorization annotations directly on each protected implementing method.

previous.context: Miren Runtime provides the runtime component for the Miren application platform. Prior to 0.11.1, the QUIC/HTTP3 RPC server on the default port 8443 uses tls.RequestClientCert and does not verify that presented certificates chain to the configured cluster certificate authority. The RPC authenticators derive a caller identity from PeerCertificates[0].Subject.CommonName without requiring a non-empty VerifiedChains value, and certificate identities bypass all RBAC checks. A network attacker who can reach the listener can present a self-signed certificate with an issuer distinguished name matching the public cluster CA subject and gain cluster superuser access, allowing disclosure, modification, or disruption of applications, sandboxes, disks, credentials, and other managed resources. This issue is fixed in version 0.11.1.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17 on Ubuntu and AlmaLinux, an unauthenticated user who obtains a valid Splunk Web session cookie before the affected user logs out could continue using the cookie after logout to access data and perform actions available to that user.
The vulnerability is possible because the logout flow does not invalidate the associated session token on affected deployments.
The attacker must obtain the valid session cookie before the affected user logs out of Splunk Web. The issue was reproduced in Splunk Enterprise installations on Ubuntu and AlmaLinux.

previous.context:
In Splunk Enterprise for Windows versions below 10.4.4, 10.2.8, 10.0.11, and 9.4.16, a user that holds a role with the edit_user capability could create multiple user accounts that share the same user directory. This could expose user-specific configuration between those accounts, let one account modify configuration used by another account, or disrupt features that depend on separate user directories.
The vulnerability is caused by improper validation of usernames before Splunk Enterprise performs Windows filesystem operations. Windows removes trailing periods from directory names, so distinct usernames can resolve to the same user directory.
For more information see Define roles on the Splunk platform with capabilities (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.6/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/define-roles-on-the-splunk-platform-with-capabilities) in the Splunk documentation.

previous.context: Flyto2 Core is an execution kernel for automation and AI-agent workflows. Prior to 2.26.8, the earlier CVE-2026-67429 remediation applied validate_path_with_env_config() to only a hand-picked set of file-writing modules, leaving data.csv.write in src/core/modules/atomic/data/csv_write.py, data.json_to_csv in src/core/modules/atomic/data/json_to_csv.py, file.copy in src/core/modules/atomic/file/copy.py, and file.move in src/core/modules/atomic/file/move.py outside the FLYTO_SANDBOX_DIR confinement boundary. The advisory also identifies unguarded modules across the broader data.*, file.*, and report-writer families. data.csv.write relies on a .. substring denylist that does not reject absolute paths, while the other named modules accept caller-controlled output or destination paths without the canonical guard. A caller able to execute modules or recipes can therefore write attacker-controlled content outside the configured sandbox, potentially overwriting application code, recipes, startup files, scheduled-task files, or authorization files and gaining code execution on the host. This issue is fixed in version 2.26.8.

previous.context: Flyto2 Core is an execution kernel for automation and AI-agent workflows. Prior to 2.26.8, validate_url_ssrf in src/core/utils.py resolves and checks a hostname but returns the hostname URL rather than the validated address, and session.get in http.get performs an independent DNS lookup when connecting. A low-privileged caller with control of the hostname's DNS can make the first lookup return a public address and the connection-time lookup return an internal address, bypassing the SSRF guard for all modules that call it and exposing readable internal or metadata-service responses. Successful exploitation requires attacker-controlled DNS and a successful timing-dependent answer change between the two lookups. This issue is fixed in version 2.26.8.

Parent-directory segments can therefore make Flyto load and execute a YAML workflow outside the bundled recipe directory, bypassing the boundary represented by list_recipes(). previous.context: Flyto2 Core is an execution kernel for automation and AI-agent workflows. Prior to 2.26.8, validate_url_ssrf() in src/core/utils.py validates one DNS answer and then returns the hostname, while guarded_aiohttp_request(), enforce_outbound_url(), and validate_url_with_env_config() allow the outbound connection to perform an independent second lookup. A caller with control of the hostname's DNS can make validation see a public address and make the connection see an internal address, bypassing the guard across its outbound consumers and exposing readable internal or metadata-service responses. The attack requires low or zero DNS TTL behavior and a successful timing-dependent answer change; static multiple-address answers are checked and do not provide the same bypass. This issue is fixed in version 2.26.8.

Issue summary: A DANE-enabled TLS client may crash by dereferencing a NULL
pointer when processing an unusual combination of certificate and TLSA
records.

Impact summary: The impact is limited to a client crash (potential Denial
of Service).

CWE: CWE-476: NULL Pointer Dereference

Description: A DANE-enabled TLS client that supports TLSA records with at
least one of the PKIX-TA(0) or PKIX-EE(1) usages alongside the DANE-TA(2)
usage may crash by dereferencing a NULL pointer if the server claims a trusted
CA's certificate to be its end-entity certificate and has an unusual mix of
associated TLSA records.

DANE SMTP clients should not be affected since only the
DANE-TA(2) and DANE-EE(3) TLSA record usages are specified applicable
in SMTP.  For example, the Postfix MTA is not affected, while the Exim
MTA does not at present use OpenSSL's DANE implementation.

Use of DANE in validation of RFC7250 raw public keys (RPKs) is also
unaffected, as these only use DANE-EE(3) TLSA records.

Only applications that support combining the DANE PKI with a traditional PKI
are potentially affected.  A DANE-enabled browser or similar, that uses
OpenSSL's DANE API could be affected.

FIPS impact: no
The DANE API is outside the FIPS module boundary.

When Apache Shiro is used with the Jakarta EE integration module, the automatic form saving feature weakens the security of a form that is resubmitted after login.
Cookies set by the application during the resubmission could lose their security attributes, such as `Secure` and `SameSite`.
In addition, the resubmitted form data and cookies could be sent to an untrusted host.
This issue affects Apache Shiro from 2.0.0-alpha through 3.0.1, only when using `shiro-jakarta-ee` integration module with form saving enabled (the default).

Mitigation: Upgrade to version 3.0.2 or later, which no longer replays the form over the network, and avoids this class of issues entirely.

previous.context:
Issue summary: Receiving crafted out-of-sequence DTLS handshake fragments may
cause OpenSSL to allocate a full message-length reassembly buffer for each
buffered message, so a small amount of wire data consumes a large amount of
memory.

Impact summary: A remote attacker can send a few small crafted DTLS handshake
fragments to make a DTLS server or client allocate well over a megabyte of
memory per connection, which may lead to memory exhaustion and Denial of
Service if many connections are made.

CWE: CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

Description: DTLS handshake messages can arrive out of order and fragmented,
so OpenSSL buffers fragments of up to ten out-of-sequence messages until
reassembly is possible. When the first fragment of a new message arrives,
OpenSSL allocates a buffer sized to the full message length declared in the
fragment header, plus a reassembly bitmap, instead of storing only the bytes
actually received. The declared length is capped by the maximum certificate
list size, 128KB by default, and that cap applies to every handshake message
type rather than only to Certificate messages.

Only DTLS endpoints reach this code. TLS, QUIC and applications that do not
use DTLS are unaffected. An attacker sends fragments that declare a large
message length but carry almost no data, using up to ten distinct message
sequence numbers.

A single connection can then hold roughly 1.4MB of buffers from about 156
bytes on the wire. Because the number of buffered messages is capped, memory
exhaustion requires many connections or many peers, which is why the severity
is Low.

FIPS impact: no
The affected code is outside the FIPS module boundary.

previous.context:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: rebind completed CREATE replays without draining the old channel

A completed DurableHandleReqV2 CREATE can be replayed through another
channel while its original channel is exiting. The existing replay path
returns the open but leaves its connection and oplock references pointing
at the old channel. Its open count also stays on that channel, and a
later CLOSE through the surviving channel decrements the wrong counter.

After checking the owner, lease key and persistent flag, verify that an
active open is still published in the requesting session's file table.
Do this even when no oplock was granted, and before processing a consumed
replay. Do not read a borrowed opinfo session pointer for this check.

Keep a healthy original binding. If the original channel is exiting or
releasing, move the open and its own oplock references to the requesting
channel. Serialize this with CLOSE using the session file-table lock,
and with detach, reconnect and notification snapshots using m_lock.
The earlier lock index and lease-table changes make their lifetimes
independent of this connection change. No old-channel r_count wait is
needed, including when an unrelated request remains active there.

Account final close against fp->conn in one place, balance durable detach
and reconnect, and transfer the count with a replay binding change. A
final global lookup put may run after CLOSE has removed the volatile id;
unlink the open from the inode list on that final close as well.

A live completed CREATE replay may follow a break that lowered the
durable open's batch oplock. Apply the batch eligibility check only to
detached reconnects, while retaining the owner, lease key and persistent
flag checks for active replays.

previous.context:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: guest_memfd: take the invalidate lock when unbinding a dying file

kvm_gmem_unbind() takes mapping->invalidate_lock only if the
get_file_active() succeeds. When the guest_memfd file is dying, its
reference count is already zero so get_file_active fails and the binding
is removed without holding the invalidate lock.

kvm_gmem_invalidate_{start,end}() checks f->bindings independently to
decide whether to begin or end KVM MMU invalidation. So, the bindings
must therefore remain stable between the two calls. Otherwise, unbind
can remove a binding after start increments mmu_invalidate_in_progress,
but before end finds the binding and decrements it.
Example, unbind race with memory failure:

  CPU 0: memory failure               CPU 1: memslot delete
  ----------------------------------  ---------------------------
                                      (guest_memfd file is dying)
  kvm_gmem_error_folio()
    kvm_gmem_invalidate_start()
      finds binding
      mmu_invalidate_in_progress++
                                      kvm_gmem_unbind()
                                        get_file_active() fails
                                        removes binding
    kvm_gmem_invalidate_end()
      no binding found
      counter stays elevated

mmu_invalidate_retry() then returns 1 forever, so guest page faults
retry without ever installing a mapping and the guest hangs.

Remove the distinction between live and dying files in the unbind path.
Always use slot->gmem.file and take the invalidate lock when it's non-NULL.
Normal unbind callers hold slots_lock, which prevents release from clearing
the pointer or freeing the file state until unbind completes. Final VM
teardown can only see a NULL pointer because guest_memfd pins the KVM until
release has cleared all bindings.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: x86: Take SRCU in kvm_zap_gfn_range()

kvm_zap_gfn_range() walks memslots and rmaps and may drop mmu_lock to
reschedule. Callers that do not already hold kvm->srcu (or slots_lock)
can race with memslot deletion: synchronize_srcu_expedited() does not
wait, kvm_free_memslot() frees the old slot and its rmap, and the zap
resumes on freed memory.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: x86/mmu: Bug the VM if KVM attempts to walk more levels than the MMU has

Extend the "EFER.LMA && !CR4.PAE" check, which exists largely to guard
against KVM configuring a paging32 MMU with more than 2 levels of paging,
with a very explicit check for exactly that: that KVM isn't trying to walk
more levels of paging than the MMU template provides.  I.e. harden KVM
against all bugs that would cause KVM to generates accesses beyond the
bounds of guest_walker's arrays, regardless of how KVM ended up with the
misconfigured MMU.

Note, don't use w->cpu_role.base.level directly as the paging64 template
only provides two levels of page tables for PAE paging on 32-bit hosts, and
handles the third level by manually emulating the PDPTR access.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: nSVM: Reject KVM_SET_NESTED_STATE if L1 has EFER.LMA=1 && EFER.LME=0

Reject KVM_SET_NESTED_STATE if the incoming L1 host state has what is
effectively an impossible EFER combination of LMA=1 but LME=0, i.e. if the
state says long mode is active but not enabled.  Unlike VMX, SVM doesn't
have an explicit consistent check for the illegal combination; presumably
hardware simply ignores EFER.LMA if EFER.LME=0.

Unfortunately, KVM doesn't ignore EFER.LMA in this case and consumes the
illegal state when constructing the shadow MMU for L2.  E.g. if userspace
also clears CR4.PAE, then kvm_calc_cpu_role() will compute a role with 4 or
5 levels of paging, but shadow_mmu_init_context() will wire up the MMU to
use the paging32 template, which maxes out its levels at 2.

Note, the "real badness" is effectively the same as what happened with the
nVMX bug fixed by commit 112e66017bff ("KVM: nVMX: add missing consistency
checks for CR0 and CR4").  Unfortunately, the sanity check added by commit
72e2fb24a0b0 ("KVM: x86/mmu: Bug the VM if a vCPU ends up in long mode
without PAE enabled") doesn't work for this case, since L2 state is active
at the time of the page fault, but it's L1 that has the bad state.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: SVM: Trigger new ASID allocation in both VMCBs on pCPU switch

When the pCPU where the VMCB was most recently used is switched, reset
the ASID generation in both VMCBs, triggering new ASID allocation for
the immediate VMRUN as well as the next VMRUN on the other VMCB.

The ASID is shared between vmcb01 and vmcb02, and gets flushed on every
nested transition. However, since pCPU tracking is done per VMCB, it is
possible for one VMCB to allocate a new ASID when migrated to a new
pCPU, and then the other VMCB reuses that ASID on the old pCPU. This can
result in the same ASID being used by multiple vCPUs on the old pCPU.

Example scenario:
- vCPU runs on pCPU A, vmcb01 is active, asid=1.
- vCPU migrates to pCPU B, vmcb01 pCPU changes, new asid=2.
- Another vCPU runs on pCPU A and allocates asid=2 as well.
- vCPU migrates back to pCPU A, and then switches to vmcb02 before it
  runs again with vmcb01.
- No pCPU switch is detected for vmcb02, so VMRUN is done with asid=2.
- Two vCPUs end up using asid=2 on the same pCPU.

Keep the VMCB dirtying to the active VMCB only. Clean bits are tracked
by a pCPU for each VMCB, so do not unnecessarily dirty a VMCB if its
pCPU does not change.

Additionally, initialize the tracked pCPU for vmcb02 to -1 on nested
enablement as hardening, so that a new ASID allocation is always
triggered when nested is disabled and re-enabled.

No performance regression was noticed when overcommitting L1 vCPUs in L0
(to force rescheduling), pinning L1 <-> L2 vCPUs, and running CPUID in a
tight loop bouncing between 2 vCPUs in L2.

An alternative (and perhaps more proper) fix would be tracking the ASID
per-VMCB instead (e.g. [1]). However, that's a more involved change, and
it would result in having different ASIDs for L1 and L2 without actually
properly maintaining them. It would probably work because all TLB
flushes target the current VMCB, and the other VMCB is always flushed on
nested transitions, but the code ends up in an arguably more fragile
state. Punt a proper clean fix to an incoming (and overdue) overhaul of
SVM's ASID usage [2].

[1] https://lore.kernel.org/lkml/20250205182402.2147495-2-yosry.ahmed@linux.dev
[2] https://lore.kernel.org/kvm/20260728003557.1136583-1-yosry@kernel.org

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

SUNRPC: fix oversized GSS proxy token copy

gss_read_proxy_verf() allocates one page per token chunk, but it copies the
entire linear head of an RPC request into in_token->pages[0]. A UDP datagram
can leave more than PAGE_SIZE bytes in the linear head, so a large
RPCSEC_GSS INIT token overwrites following pages.

Copy the linear head in page-sized chunks before switching to the request
page array. The linear head itself can span multiple pages.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

SUNRPC: Do not credit control-record octets to the RPC stream

svc_tcp_sock_recv_cmsg() receives up to two octets into a local
buffer, and returns that count for any record type other than
TLS_RECORD_TYPE_ALERT. Nothing reached the caller's buffer, but
svc_tcp_read_marker() adds the count to sk_tcplen and
svc_tcp_read_msg()'s caller adds it to sk_datalen. The RPC stream
advances over octets it never received. The fragment marker is
assembled from stale sk_marker octets. The message body comes from
pages nothing wrote.

A conforming client reaches this. RFC 8446 Section 4.6.3 lets either
peer send KeyUpdate once it has sent its Finished, and svcsock has no
rekey path. kTLS leaves the partially consumed record on ctx->rx_list,
so the body drains two octets per svc_tcp_recvfrom() call. Each pair
is credited the same way.

Return -EAGAIN for a record that is not an alert. That is what
svc_tcp_sock_process_cmsg()'s default arm returned before the receive
moved into a local buffer.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

nfsd: preflight SEQUENCE replies before accepting a slot

nfsd4_sequence() narrows the reply buffer to the session's cached
reply limit before it accepts the slot seqid. A client may negotiate
ca_maxresponsesize_cached down to NFSD_MIN_HDR_SEQ_SZ, and
nfsd4_alloc_slot() then gives every slot a zero-length sl_data[]. A
COMPOUND tag can fill that narrowed buffer until it holds the
SEQUENCE opcode but not the status word that follows.
nfsd4_encode_operation() returns without running
nfsd4_encode_sequence(), so cstate.data_offset stays zero. It leaves
op->status at nfs_ok as well, so the COMPOUND is treated as having
succeeded.

nfsd4_store_cache_entry() declines to cache a lone SEQUENCE that
returned an error. That test reads the status the operation
reported, so it passes here. The copy starts at offset zero and
takes the whole reply, RPC and COMPOUND headers included, into the
zero-length sl_data[]. The COMPOUND tag is copied along with it, so
the client picks most of the bytes written past the end of the slot:

  BUG: KASAN: slab-out-of-bounds in read_bytes_from_xdr_buf+0x1bc/0x390
  Write of size 80 at addr ffff888003a549cd by task kunit_try_catch/24
   __asan_memcpy+0x38/0x60
   read_bytes_from_xdr_buf+0x1bc/0x390
   nfsd4_sequence_done+0x5b0/0x810
   nfs4svc_encode_compoundres+0x1bf/0x240

Check that the fixed-size SEQUENCE result, plus room for a following
operation's error status, fits the negotiated limit before narrowing
the buffer and consuming the slot seqid. The slot and its reply
cache are left unchanged, as RFC 8881 Section 2.10.6.1.2 requires of
an error returned from SEQUENCE.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

nfsd: don't modify a session slot when replaying its cached reply

nfsd4_sequence() claims a session slot by setting NFSD4_SLOT_INUSE
under nn->client_lock. A reply served from the slot's reply cache does
not claim it, and that distinction lived only in cstate->status, which
nfsd4_sequence() set to nfserr_replay_cache. Commit cc028a10a48c
("NFSD: Hoist status code encoding into XDR encoder functions") moved
nfsd4_proc_compound()'s cstate->status assignment below the out:
label, and the replay path's goto out was the one path that relied on
skipping it. The test in nfsd4_sequence_done() therefore no longer
identifies a replay, and every replay now stores its reply and clears
NFSD4_SLOT_INUSE as though it owned the slot.

NFSD4_SLOT_INUSE is the interlock: check_slot_seqid() rejects every
sequence id for a slot that is in use, before replay_matches_cache()
runs. A replay never sets it, so two replays can be in flight on the
same slot at once. One can read slot->sl_cred under nn->client_lock
while the other's completion frees and rebuilds it from the XDR
encoder without that lock. Two completions can also collide with each
other and release the same group_info twice. free_svc_cred() leaves
cr_uid, cr_gid and cr_flavor intact, so the reader passes every
earlier test in same_creds() and dereferences a NULL cr_group_info.
From a 6.12.91 production server:

  BUG: kernel NULL pointer dereference, address: 0000000000000004
  CPU: 63 UID: 0 PID: 39015 Comm: nfsd
  RIP: 0010:same_creds+0x38/0xa0 [nfsd]
  RDX: 0000000000000000
  Call Trace:
   nfsd4_sequence+0x6a8/0x910 [nfsd]
   nfsd4_proc_compound+0x345/0x670 [nfsd]
   nfsd_dispatch+0x100/0x220 [nfsd]
   svc_process_common+0x311/0x700 [sunrpc]
   svc_process+0x131/0x1c0 [sunrpc]
   svc_recv+0x7ef/0x9c0 [sunrpc]
   nfsd+0xa3/0x100 [nfsd]
  Kernel panic - not syncing: Fatal exception

Since v6.14 a live session's slot table can shrink, and the unowned
store becomes a use-after-free write. nfsd4_sequence() defers the
shrink while a slot is in use, but it tests NFSD4_SLOT_INUSE, which a
replay does not set, so free_session_slots() can kfree() the slot the
replay still holds in cstate->slot.

Record the claim in cstate->slot_owned when nfsd4_sequence() accepts a
request and test that in nfsd4_sequence_done(), so only the request
that claimed the slot updates its cached reply and clears
NFSD4_SLOT_INUSE. svc_generic_init_request() zeroes the compound
response before each request, so the flag starts clear.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

NFSD: copy SETXATTR data from all XDR buffer segments

nfsd4_vbuf_from_vector() manually copies the head followed by whole
pages starting at offset zero. This assumes that all remaining data
starts at the beginning of the page array and that no data is stored
in the tail.

However, nfsd4_decode_setxattr() passes an xdr_buf returned by
xdr_stream_subsegment(). Such a sub-buffer can have a nonzero
page_base and can span its page and tail segments. Ignoring that
layout can copy the wrong bytes into the value passed to
vfs_setxattr().

Use read_bytes_from_xdr_buf(), which observes the complete xdr_buf
layout.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: validate SMB1 EA list bounds before parsing

CIFSSMBQAllEAs() checks the server-provided EA list length by adding it
to the response pointer. On 32-bit systems, a positive length can wrap
the pointer and pass the comparison. The parser then walks outside the
received response while reading the next FEA header.

A response with a list length of 0x40000000 reproduces this as a native
i386 page fault and kernel panic from listxattr() against an SMB1
server.

Check that the EA list starts within the SMB byte area before reading
its header. Keep its length unsigned and compare it with the bytes left
in the response without pointer addition.

SMB1 is not negotiated by default and requires an explicit vers=1.0
mount.

smb: client: validate NT transaction response layout and offsets

validate_ntransact() assumes that the response uses the fixed 18-word NT
transaction layout. A different WordCount makes get_bcc() locate the byte
count at a different offset from pSMBr->ByteCount, allowing the subsequent
bounds checks to use inconsistent response boundaries.

into pointers before checking their bounds. On a 32-bit client, a large
offset can wrap the pointer below end_of_smb and pass the one-sided pointer
comparison. The caller then dereferences the parameter pointer or copies
from the data pointer.

Require the expected WordCount before reading the byte count. Check each
offset and count against the received SMB length as integers before forming
either pointer. Use subtraction after validating the offset so that the
range checks cannot overflow.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: reclaim credits for decrypted reads with no matching mid

When a decrypted SMB2 READ response carries a MessageId that matches no
outstanding request, both the inline receive_encrypted_read() and the
offloaded smb2_decrypt_offload() paths drop the frame without accounting
the credits the server granted in it.  The plaintext unknown-frame path in
cifs_demultiplex_thread() already reclaims them with
smb2_add_credits_from_hdr(), so encrypted reads leak credits that the
plaintext path would not.

This also happens for legitimate frames - e.g. a reply that arrives after
the client has timed out and dropped the mid - so over a long-lived
connection the client's credit count drifts down and can eventually starve
it of the ability to issue requests.  The frame is AEAD-authenticated, so
the granted credits in the decrypted header come from the real server and
are safe to apply.

Reclaim the credits from the decrypted header before dropping the frame,
and export smb2_add_credits_from_hdr() so the SMB2 receive paths can use it.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: fix buffer overflow in SMB2_tcon()

In SMB2_tcon(), unc_path is allocated with a fixed buffer size of
MAX_SHARENAME_LENGTH * 2 bytes (672 bytes). However, the user-controlled
UNC path (tree) length is passed to cifs_strtoUTF16(), which assumes the
destination buffer is large enough and writes strlen(tree) + 1 UTF-16 code
units.

Commit 62a1a439e0fd ("cifs: clean up handling of unc= option") removed the
length check on UNC mount options, allowing mount paths to exceed
MAX_SHARENAME_LENGTH while retaining the fixed-size buffer allocation in
SMB2_tcon(). Consequently, an oversized UNC string causes cifs_strtoUTF16()
to write past the end of the heap object, resulting in a slab-out-of-bounds
write. Furthermore, if a tree exceeds MAX_TREE_SIZE characters, strscpy()
truncates it in cifs_tcon::tree_name, causing subsequent reconnects or
failovers to fail.

Fix this by first verifying that the length of tree does not exceed
MAX_TREE_SIZE, returning -EINVAL if it does. Then, dynamically allocate
unc_path based on the length of tree so that it safely accommodates all
UTF-16 code units for paths within MAX_TREE_SIZE.

[pc: remove unused MAX_SHARENAME_LENGTH]
